collection: Ndovera original WAEC/JAMB Literature in English — batch 035
note: All examples, prose passages, poems and scenes are original and invented. 50 WAEC and 50 JAMB four-option drafts. General knowledge and unseen appreciation only, not whole examination papers. Official WAEC 2026–2030 selected-work list is separately registered but this batch includes no prescribed-text essays or Shakespeare contexts. Full current official syllabus verification and independent academic approval remain outstanding.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.learningObjective: Identify a literary device in an original example and explain its effect.
questions.prompt: In the original sentence “The news struck her like a stone against a window”, the comparison primarily suggests
questions.answer: a sudden, disturbing impact.
options: a carefully measured exchange.
a quiet, gradual reassurance.
a deliberate physical attack on a real window.
a sudden, disturbing impact.
questions.explanation: The explicit like-comparison transfers the shock of a stone hitting glass to the effect of news.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.learningObjective: Identify a literary device in an original example and explain its effect.
questions.prompt: A speaker calls the community library “a harbour for restless minds”. The metaphor presents reading as
questions.answer: a source of refuge and support for thought.
options: a means of transporting goods by water.
a source of refuge and support for thought.
a guarantee that all uncertainty disappears forever.
an activity possible only beside the sea.
questions.explanation: Harbour is transferred from a place of shelter for boats to the library’s intellectual and emotional role.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.learningObjective: Identify a literary device in an original example and explain its effect.
questions.prompt: Which device is most evident in “Dawn tiptoed through the shutters”?
questions.answer: Personification.
options: Allusion.
A rhetorical question.
Euphemism.
Personification.
questions.explanation: Dawn is given the human action of moving on tiptoe.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.learningObjective: Identify a literary device in an original example and explain its effect.
questions.prompt: “I have corrected this sentence a million times,” a tired editor says after several revisions. The exaggeration chiefly conveys
questions.answer: frustration with repeated effort.
options: frustration with repeated effort.
an exact record of the revision count.
a comparison between two kinds of punctuation.
the editor’s confidence that no changes were needed.
questions.explanation: The implausibly large number intensifies frustration rather than supplying literal data.

questions.subject: Literature in English

questions.prompt: Which expression contains an oxymoron?

options: A memory that slowly fades.
A memory of a quiet street.
A memory from last year.
A painfully pleasant memory.
questions.explanation: Painfully and pleasant bring apparently contradictory qualities into one compact expression.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.learningObjective: Identify a literary device in an original example and explain its effect.
questions.prompt: A chairman says, “Everyone must be heard,” then switches off the microphone whenever anyone disagrees. The irony lies chiefly in
questions.answer: the contradiction between his declared principle and his conduct.
options: the fact that a meeting has a chairman.
the use of a microphone in a public setting.
the absence of an audience at the meeting.
the contradiction between his declared principle and his conduct.
questions.explanation: The actions undermine the promise of open participation.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.learningObjective: Identify a literary device in an original example and explain its effect.
questions.prompt: A cracked cup appears when a family separates and again when reconciliation begins. Its recurring use most plausibly makes it
questions.answer: a symbol of a damaged relationship that may be repaired.
options: a narrator with independent knowledge of events.
a rhyme scheme connecting the two scenes.
a symbol of a damaged relationship that may be repaired.
proof that the story is a technical guide to pottery.
questions.explanation: The object acquires a significance beyond its practical function through its repeated connection with the relationship.

questions.subject: Literature in English

questions.prompt: Early in a story, the narrator briefly notices a bridge plank lifting under a passing cart. Much later the bridge fails. The early detail functions as
questions.answer: foreshadowing.
options: an interruption by a new narrator.
a final resolution.
a retrospective summary after the failure.
foreshadowing.

a change from prose to dialogue as a genre.
the final resolution of the reunion.
a flashback.

questions.subject: Literature in English

questions.subject: Literature in English

indirect characterisation through behaviour.

questions.subject: Literature in English

questions.prompt: A fictional official is generous to relatives, harsh towards employees and privately ashamed of his behaviour. These contrasting qualities most directly support describing him as

a round character.
questions.explanation: Several conflicting dimensions give the character complexity; complexity alone does not prove change over time.

questions.prompt: Which account most clearly presents a causal plot rather than merely a sequence?

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an original prose extract through textual evidence and narrative technique.
questions.prompt: What does Sade’s repeated hiding of the letter most strongly suggest?
questions.answer: She is uncertain how her plans will be received.
options: She intends to sell the letter to a customer.
She is uncertain how her plans will be received.
She has already discussed every detail with her mother.
She cannot recognise the language of the letter.
questions.explanation: Her concealment, repeated reading and prepared argument indicate apprehension about a response.
questions.passage: Sade placed the letter beneath a length of blue cloth whenever a customer entered. By noon she had read the first line so often that the paper had softened at the fold. Her mother worked the sewing machine without asking about it. Last month, when Sade mentioned the design scholarship, her mother had counted the unfinished uniforms and said nothing. Now the machine stopped. Sade prepared her argument about earning money while studying, but her mother reached into a biscuit tin and brought out a tape measure. Its numbers had faded where years of fingers had held it. “You will need one of your own,” she said. Sade unfolded the letter. For the first time that morning, she read beyond the word “Congratulations”. Outside, someone called for a uniform; neither woman answered immediately.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an original prose extract through textual evidence and narrative technique.
questions.prompt: The contrast between imagined applause and actual silence chiefly reveals
questions.answer: the difference between anticipated success and the anxiety of beginning.
options: the audience’s deliberate plan to destroy the drum.
the narrator’s dislike of every form of music.
the uncle’s refusal to let the narrator perform.
the difference between anticipated success and the anxiety of beginning.
questions.explanation: The narrator imagined recognition but had not prepared emotionally for the exposed moment before playing.
questions.passage: I arrived at the square carrying the drum my uncle had lent me. All week I had imagined the applause after my first solo. I had not imagined the silence before it. The other drummers waited beneath the neem tree, their hands resting on their instruments. Someone shifted a bench. Someone coughed. I tightened a rope that needed no tightening. When my uncle nodded, I struck the opening pattern too quickly. The older players did not correct me aloud; they slowed their own beat until I could find it. Only then did the faces in front of us separate into people I knew. Afterwards, my uncle asked whether I had enjoyed playing alone. I began to say yes, then looked at the men packing their drums beside mine. “Not quite alone,” I said.

questions.prompt: What does tightening a rope that needs no tightening imply about the narrator?
questions.answer: Nervousness is finding expression in an unnecessary action.
options: The performance has already ended successfully.
The narrator is correcting the older drummers’ instruments.
The borrowed drum has certainly broken beyond repair.
Nervousness is finding expression in an unnecessary action.
questions.explanation: The explicit absence of need makes the action a sign of unease rather than routine repair.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.subtopic: Poetic voice imagery sound and structure
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an original poem by relating language and structure to meaning.
questions.prompt: In “the washing line writes white”, the image chiefly transforms the drying clothes into
questions.answer: marks made across the space of the yard.
options: a description of rain dissolving ink.
marks made across the space of the yard.
evidence that the yard has been painted permanently.
a literal letter written by a bus driver.
questions.explanation: Writes turns the visual arrangement of pale washing into an act of inscription.
questions.passage:
At dawn the washing line writes white across the yard.
Shirts lift their empty arms towards the road;
I pin my father’s coat beside my school dress,
and watch the sleeves grow restless in the wind.
Beyond our wall, the buses gather speed.
My dress leans outward, held by two small pegs.

questions.prompt: Which loss matters most to Binta as the passage presents it?
questions.answer: The familiar social rhythm attached to the cinema.

questions.explanation: The absent queue and familiar paired arrivals show the loss of a shared routine, beyond a change in building use.
questions.passage: The old cinema became a furniture store in August. Binta, who had sold groundnuts by its doorway for twenty years, watched the painted stars disappear beneath a coat of cream. On the first Saturday, she set out her tray at the usual hour. No queue formed. A delivery driver asked whether she could move so that his men could carry in a wardrobe. She shifted to the shade of a mango tree. From there she could still see the doorway, but it no longer framed the familiar faces arriving in pairs. At sunset the new owner brought out a chair. “You might be more comfortable,” he said. Binta thanked him and sat. For years she had wanted a place to rest during the interval. Now the interval seemed to have swallowed the entire evening.

questions.answer: the limits of general information for a particular personal need.

The map spread on the hospital desk
knows every road except the one I need.
Its rivers run in blue, its borders straight;
my father’s ward is down a nameless turn.
A cleaner points with one wet, yellow glove.
I follow, folding cities out of sight,
until the paper fits inside my palm
and there is only one door left to find.
